title: How Do You Find and Use Sermon Illustrations?
subtitle: An illustration is a window, not decoration: how to find them, how to use them, and the kinds that betray the text

sections.title: A Window, Not a Decoration
sections.body:
Most preachers misuse illustrations because they misunderstand what they are. They treat the story as ornament, a bit of relief hung on the wall of an argument to keep people awake.

An illustration is not decoration. It is a window.

A window exists for one reason, to let light into a room that was dark, to let people see something they could not see through the wall of the bare proposition. The doctrine of grace is true and abstract and easy to nod at. The story of a father running down the road toward a son who wasted everything, that story is a window, and through it people suddenly see grace and feel it land. The illustration that calls attention to itself is a stained-glass window in a room that needed plain light. You remember the cleverness and forget the truth it was supposed to show you. I have preached illustrations people loved and remembered, and a week later they could not tell you what the illustration was for, which means it was not a window. It was a mirror, and they were looking at me.

sections.title: Where to Find Them
sections.body:
The best illustrations are not found in books of illustrations. Those are pre-chewed and bloodless, the same dozen stories every preacher has used until they are worn smooth and unbelievable.

The best ones come from paying attention to the actual world. So pay attention.

Watch your own life, your kitchen, your kids, your failures, and especially your failures, because the preacher who can name his own sin honestly has found the most disarming window there is. Read widely outside the Bible, history and biography and the news and the novel, because a preacher who only reads sermons has nothing to look through but other people's windows. Notice the way ordinary work actually works, the way a nurse changes a dressing, the way a farmer waits on rain he cannot summon, the way grief moves through a house. Keep a file. When something opens a truth to you, write it down that day, because you will not remember it on Thursday when you need it. Build the file all year, not the night before. The preacher with a full file preaches from abundance. The preacher with an empty file reaches for the same tired story about the lighthouse and the ship, and everyone has heard it, and no light gets in.

sections.title: How to Use Them Well
sections.body:
Once you have a window, you have to hang it right, and craft matters here as much as content. The mistake is to over-explain, to tell the story and then crush it by spelling out exactly what it means.

Trust the story to do its work. A window you have to narrate is a window you have painted over.

Keep illustrations short and pointed. The story that runs five minutes to illuminate a one-minute truth has become the master rather than the servant, and the congregation now remembers the tale and not the text. Use one good window per point, not five, because a wall of windows is just glass and the light has nowhere to land. Place it where the people most need to see, at the moment the abstract has gone foggy and they need to look through to something solid. And know when to use no illustration at all, because some truths are clearest when stated plainly and bare, and a story at that moment would only get in the way. The goal is never that they admire your stories. The goal is that they see the truth so clearly through the story that they forget the glass was ever there.

sections.title: The Kinds That Betray the Text
sections.body:
Some illustrations do not let light in. They distort it, or they put it on the wrong thing, and these you must learn to refuse no matter how good the story is.

An illustration that betrays the text is worse than no illustration at all, because it teaches a falsehood with the force of a picture.

Refuse the story that is too good, the one so dramatic the congregation spends the rest of the sermon thinking about it instead of God. Refuse the story that makes you the hero, because the preacher who is always the wise one in his own illustrations is building a monument to himself, and they can feel it even when they cannot name it. Refuse the story that is not true, the embellished anecdote, the it happened to a friend that did not happen to anyone, because a preacher who fudges a story will be suspected of fudging the gospel, and that suspicion is fair. Refuse the illustration that flatters the room, that lets your people feel superior to some absent fool, because that is not a window onto grace, it is a mirror for pride. And refuse the one that distorts the doctrine, that wins the moment by teaching something the text does not say. The cleverest illustration in the world is not worth a single false note about who God is. The window serves the text. The day it competes with the text, take it down.

sections.title: The One Who Taught in Pictures
sections.body:
If you want to learn this craft, sit at the feet of the one who did it best, and he did not preach in propositions. He preached in windows.

Jesus told stories. A sower, a pearl, a lost coin, a wayward son. The deepest theology ever spoken came as pictures of ordinary life.

Notice what he did. He took the world his hearers already knew, seeds and soil and debts and bread, and he made it a window onto the kingdom of God. He did not always explain. Sometimes he left the parable standing and let it do its slow work, let it lodge in people and detonate later. He was never the hero of his own stories, and his stories never flattered the religious people listening, which is exactly why they wanted him dead. Learn from him. Let your windows come from the world your people actually live in. Let them be honest. Let them point away from you and toward the only one worth seeing. The point of every window you hang was never the glass. It was the light, and the light has a name, and your whole job is to get out of its way so they can see it.
